summary: Ten young Florentines, seven women and three men, leave plague-struck Florence for a country villa. To pass the time they agree that each will tell one story a day for ten days, and the book gathers all one hundred tales. A king or queen is chosen each day and sets the theme: fortune, will, unhappy love, happy love, quick replies, tricks played by wives, and generous deeds. The stories run from bawdy jokes to tragedy, and Dioneo is free to pick any topic.
context: Boccaccio wrote the book in Florentine vernacular prose, probably between 1348 and 1353, in the shadow of the Black Death. Most of the tales were older than he was, and he gave them his own style. Chaucer drew on it for The Canterbury Tales. The first recorded translation into another language was a Catalan manuscript made at Sant Cugat in 1429. Later writers kept reworking the stories, and the site carries John Payne's English version from the Standard Ebooks edition.

people.name: Giovanni Boccaccio
people.note: Italian writer and humanist, born in Certaldo in 1313 and dead in 1375.

people.name: John Payne
people.note: Made the English translation in the Standard Ebooks edition.

people.name: Dioneo
people.note: One of the three young men, who is allowed to pick any topic and usually tells the tenth tale of each day.

people.name: Ser Ciappelletto
people.note: The villain of the first tale, who is mistaken for a saint after his death.

people.name: Petrarch
people.note: Boccaccio's friend and teacher, whose letter version of a tale served as a source for translators.

people.name: Dante Alighieri
people.note: Boccaccio named Dante's Comedy 'Divine' and copied its manuscripts.

people.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
people.note: English poet influenced by the Decameron's tales.

places.name: Florence
places.note: The city the ten storytellers flee when the Black Death strikes.

places.name: Fiesole
places.note: The countryside villa where the company shelters and tells its tales.

places.name: Certaldo
places.note: Boccaccio's birthplace, from which he took the nickname the Certaldese.

places.name: Sant Cugat del Valles
places.note: Site of the first recorded foreign translation, a Catalan manuscript of 1429.

timeline.label: The Black Death strikes Florence, the setting of the frame story and the likely start of composition.
The Decameron is thought to be finished by about this year.
A Catalan manuscript becomes the first recorded translation into another language.
Apostolo Zeno writes the libretto Griselda, drawn from the last tale.
G. H. McWilliam publishes a complete English translation.

ideas.title: Storytelling against the plague
ideas.note: The frame story shows ten people choosing order and conversation while death spreads through the city.

ideas.title: One theme each day
ideas.note: Each day has a ruler who sets a topic, such as fortune, wit or generosity, which gives the hundred tales a shape.

ideas.title: Vernacular prose as art
ideas.note: Boccaccio wrote in Florentine, and later critics treated his style as a model of Italian prose.

ideas.title: Everyday life in tales
ideas.note: The stories give a picture of daily life in fourteenth-century Italy.
